name: Saransh Singh
role: Final-year ECE student working on offensive security, mobile and hardware.
about: I'm Saransh Singh, a final-year Electronics and Communication Engineering student at DCRUST Murthal, India, and Cybersecurity Lead for the 2026 batch. I started on the blue-team side — logs, kill chains, indicators — and now spend most of my time on offence: mobile application testing, hardware security and drone authentication.

I learn by building. A BLE HID framework on an ESP32-S3, an authentication scheme that rebuilds its key from silicon instead of storing one, a scanner that keeps working inside RASP-protected Android apps. Each one ends with a write-up that says what works, what doesn't, and what I would do differently.

pillars.label: Build
pillars.body: Offensive tooling, mobile app assessments, ESP32 firmware and the occasional desktop environment.

pillars.label: Explore
pillars.body: Android internals, BLE, physical unclonable functions, and the places where hardware and app security meet.

pillars.label: Improve
pillars.body: Report quality, reproducible testing, and the habit of proving a finding rather than assuming it.

projects.name: Mayavi
projects.description: BLE HID emulation and keystroke framework for the ESP32-S3, with a Wi-Fi dashboard served from the device itself.
bullets: Configurable HID payloads over Bluetooth Low Energy
On-board web dashboard, no host software required
C++ firmware built on the Arduino and ESP-IDF toolchain

projects.name: PUF drone authentication
projects.description: Hardware-rooted UAV authentication. SRAM PUFs and BCH fuzzy extractors rebuild a 128-bit secret from silicon variation, so no key sits in flash.
bullets: Single-use nonce HMAC handshake between drone and ground station
A firmware dump yields public helper data and nothing else
ESP32 firmware in C, Flask command dashboard

projects.name: Drax
projects.description: Mobile app security scanner: a Python core plus an Android agent over ADB, built to keep working inside RASP-protected apps.
bullets: About 50 checks across static, dynamic and Frida-based testing
Scope-limited by design: authorised assessments only
Not public, so this card says so instead of linking nowhere

projects.name: Quarters
projects.description: Open, self-hostable virtual HQ: a pixel-art world with proximity voice and video, and Discord-style spaces.
bullets: Proximity audio and video that react to where you stand
Self-hostable: one deploy for a whole team
Built as a workspace rather than a video call

projects.name: SaviOS desktop
projects.description: A reproducible Arch desktop: packages, CachyOS kernel and Hyprland configuration from one shell-scripted source of truth.
bullets: Idempotent install script, rebuildable from scratch
Hyprland, Quickshell bar and a matched terminal stack
Also kept as cachyos-env for tuned hardware

projects.name: More repositories
projects.description: Coursework, forensic lab notes, networking references and other experiments that did not make the shortlist.
bullets: networking-vault: a site for learning networking
Labs and grc-portfolio: class work and governance notes

focus: Metasploit, Kali Linux, Android pentesting, PortSwigger labs (SQLi, XSS, SSRF, LLM prompt injection)
ADB, Frida, SSL pinning and root detection, RASP-protected apps
ESP32 and ESP32-S3, ESP-IDF, BLE, SRAM PUFs, BCH error correction
Log analysis, kill-chain mapping, IoC extraction

how.title: Authorised scope only.
how.body: Drax exists for assessments on apps I own or have been engaged to test. The README says that before it says anything else.

how.title: Ask what the attacker gets.
how.body: For the PUF drone design the question was what a firmware dump reveals. The answer is public helper data and nothing else.

how.title: Say what's private.
how.body: Drax isn't public, so its card says PRIVATE instead of linking nowhere. Claims stay checkable.

how.title: Write it up.
how.body: Lab reports and READMEs get the same care as the code: setup, limits, evidence.

priorities: Turn the PUF work into a measurement-backed write-up rather than a demo.
Publish sanitised Drax findings so the methodology is readable without the tool.
Build more blue-team detection queries and test them against real logs.
Contribute upstream to tools I already depend on: Frida scripts, ESP-IDF examples, Ryoku.
